claim: The human brain represents 2% of the body mass.
source: The human brain represents 2% of the body mass, yet it consumes about 20% of blood oxygen and glucose which are mandatory energy substrates (Clarke and Sokoloff, 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to Clarke and Sokoloff, 1999

claim: The human brain consumes about 20% of blood oxygen and glucose.
source: The human brain represents 2% of the body mass, yet it consumes about 20% of blood oxygen and glucose which are mandatory energy substrates (Clarke and Sokoloff, 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to Clarke and Sokoloff, 1999

claim: Oxygen and glucose are mandatory energy substrates for the brain.
source: The human brain represents 2% of the body mass, yet it consumes about 20% of blood oxygen and glucose which are mandatory energy substrates (Clarke and Sokoloff, 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to Clarke and Sokoloff, 1999

claim: The majority (~50–80%) of cerebral energy metabolism is consumed by the Na+/K+ ATPase pump.
source: The majority (~50–80%) of the cerebral energy metabolism is believed to be consumed by the Na+/K+ ATPase pump to maintain cellular ionic gradients dissipated during synaptic transmission and action potentials (Attwell and Laughlin, 2001; Lennie, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to Attwell and Laughlin, 2001 and Lennie, 2003

claim: The Na+/K+ ATPase pump maintains cellular ionic gradients dissipated during synaptic transmission and action potentials.
source: The majority (~50–80%) of the cerebral energy metabolism is believed to be consumed by the Na+/K+ ATPase pump to maintain cellular ionic gradients dissipated during synaptic transmission and action potentials (Attwell and Laughlin, 2001; Lennie, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to Attwell and Laughlin, 2001 and Lennie, 2003

claim: Synaptic and spiking activities are coupled with local cerebral blood flow and glucose uptake.
source: Synaptic and spiking activities are also coupled with local cerebral blood flow and glucose uptake (Devor et al., 2008; Logothetis, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Devor et al., 2008 and Logothetis, 2008

claim: Neurovascular and neurometabolic coupling is the physiological basis of brain imaging techniques.
source: This process, referred to as neurovascular and neurometabolic coupling, is the physiological basis of brain imaging techniques (Raichle and Mintun, 2006) and maintains extracellular glucose within a physiological range of 2–3 mM (Silver and Erecińska, 1994; Hu and Wilson, 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Raichle and Mintun, 2006

claim: Neurovascular and neurometabolic coupling maintains extracellular glucose within a physiological range of 2–3 mM.
source: This process, referred to as neurovascular and neurometabolic coupling, is the physiological basis of brain imaging techniques (Raichle and Mintun, 2006) and maintains extracellular glucose within a physiological range of 2–3 mM (Silver and Erecińska, 1994; Hu and Wilson, 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to Silver and Erecińska, 1994 and Hu and Wilson, 2002

claim: Following increased neuronal activity, extracellular lactate increases for several minutes up to twice of its 2–5 mM basal concentration despite oxygen availability.
source: Also, following increased neuronal activity extracellular lactate increases (Prichard et al., 1991; Hu and Wilson, 1997) for several minutes up to twice of its 2–5 mM basal concentration despite oxygen availability (Magistretti and Allaman, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Prichard et al., 1991, Hu and Wilson, 1997, and Magistretti and Allaman, 2018

claim: A lactate gradient exists between astrocytes and neurons.
source: This hypothesis is supported by the existence of a lactate gradient between astrocytes and neurons (Mächler et al., 2016), the preferential use of lactate as an energy substrate in cultured neurons (Bouzier-Sore et al., 2003; Bouzier-Sore et al., 2006), and its ability to support neuronal activity during glucose shortage (Schurr et al., 1988; Rouach et al., 2008; Wyss et al., 2011; Choi et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mächler et al., 2016

claim: Cultured neurons preferentially use lactate as an energy substrate.
source: This hypothesis is supported by the existence of a lactate gradient between astrocytes and neurons (Mächler et al., 2016), the preferential use of lactate as an energy substrate in cultured neurons (Bouzier-Sore et al., 2003; Bouzier-Sore et al., 2006), and its ability to support neuronal activity during glucose shortage (Schurr et al., 1988; Rouach et al., 2008; Wyss et al., 2011; Choi et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bouzier-Sore et al., 2003 and Bouzier-Sore et al., 2006

claim: Lactate can support neuronal activity during glucose shortage.
source: This hypothesis is supported by the existence of a lactate gradient between astrocytes and neurons (Mächler et al., 2016), the preferential use of lactate as an energy substrate in cultured neurons (Bouzier-Sore et al., 2003; Bouzier-Sore et al., 2006), and its ability to support neuronal activity during glucose shortage (Schurr et al., 1988; Rouach et al., 2008; Wyss et al., 2011; Choi et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Schurr et al., 1988; Rouach et al., 2008; Wyss et al., 2011; Choi et al., 2012

claim: Brain slices and in vivo evidence indicate that synaptic and sensory stimulation enhanced neuronal glycolysis and potentially lactate release by neurons.
source: Furthermore, brain slices and in vivo evidence have indicated that synaptic and sensory stimulation enhanced neuronal glycolysis and potentially lactate release by neurons (Ivanov et al., 2014; Díaz-García et al., 2017), thereby challenging the astrocyte–neuron lactate shuttle hypothesis.
evidence: Supported by citations to Ivanov et al., 2014 and Díaz-García et al., 2017

claim: KATP channels act as metabolic sensors controlling various cellular functions.
source: ATP-sensitive potassium channels (KATP) act as metabolic sensors controlling various cellular functions (Babenko et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation to Babenko et al., 1998

claim: The open probability of KATP channels is regulated by the energy charge of the cell (i.e., the ATP/ADP ratio).
source: Their open probability (po) is regulated by the energy charge of the cell (i.e., the ATP/ADP ratio).
evidence: Based on established knowledge of KATP channel function

claim: ATP mediates a tonic background inhibition of KATP channels.
source: While ATP mediates a tonic background inhibition of KATP channels, cytosolic increases of ADP concentrations that occur as a sequel to enhanced energy demands, increase the po of KATP channels.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of KATP channel regulation

claim: Cytosolic increases of ADP concentrations increase the open probability of KATP channels.
source: While ATP mediates a tonic background inhibition of KATP channels, cytosolic increases of ADP concentrations that occur as a sequel to enhanced energy demands, increase the po of KATP channels.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of KATP channel regulation

claim: In neurons, electrical activity is accompanied by enhanced sodium influx, which in turn activates the Na+/K+ ATPase.
source: In neurons, electrical activity is accompanied by enhanced sodium influx, which in turn activates the Na+/K+ ATPase.
evidence: Based on established neurophysiological knowledge

claim: Activity of the Na+/K+ ATPase alters the submembrane ATP/ADP ratio sufficiently to activate KATP channels.
source: Activity of this pump alters the submembrane ATP/ADP ratio sufficiently to activate KATP channels (Tanner et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tanner et al., 2011

claim: KATP channels are activated (po > 0.1) when ATP/ADP ratio is ≤5.
source: The use of fluorescent ATP/ADP biosensors has demonstrated that KATP channels are activated (po > 0.1) when ATP/ADP ratio is ≤5 (Tantama et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tantama et al., 2013

claim: KATP channel subunits are expressed in the neocortex.
source: KATP channel subunits are expressed in the neocortex (Ashford et al., 1988; Karschin et al., 1997; Dunn-Meynell et al., 1998; Thomzig et al., 2005; Cahoy et al., 2008; Zeisel et al., 2015; Tasic et al., 2016) and have been shown to protect cortical neurons from ischemic injury (Héron-Milhavet et al., 2004; Sun et al., 2006) and to modulate their excitability (Giménez-Cassina et al., 2012) and intrinsic firing activity (Lemak et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: KATP channels protect cortical neurons from ischemic injury.
source: KATP channel subunits are expressed in the neocortex (Ashford et al., 1988; Karschin et al., 1997; Dunn-Meynell et al., 1998; Thomzig et al., 2005; Cahoy et al., 2008; Zeisel et al., 2015; Tasic et al., 2016) and have been shown to protect cortical neurons from ischemic injury (Héron-Milhavet et al., 2004; Sun et al., 2006) and to modulate their excitability (Giménez-Cassina et al., 2012) and intrinsic firing activity (Lemak et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Héron-Milhavet et al., 2004 and Sun et al., 2006

claim: KATP channels modulate the excitability of cortical neurons.
source: KATP channel subunits are expressed in the neocortex (Ashford et al., 1988; Karschin et al., 1997; Dunn-Meynell et al., 1998; Thomzig et al., 2005; Cahoy et al., 2008; Zeisel et al., 2015; Tasic et al., 2016) and have been shown to protect cortical neurons from ischemic injury (Héron-Milhavet et al., 2004; Sun et al., 2006) and to modulate their excitability (Giménez-Cassina et al., 2012) and intrinsic firing activity (Lemak et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Giménez-Cassina et al., 2012

claim: KATP channels modulate the intrinsic firing activity of cortical neurons.
source: KATP channel subunits are expressed in the neocortex (Ashford et al., 1988; Karschin et al., 1997; Dunn-Meynell et al., 1998; Thomzig et al., 2005; Cahoy et al., 2008; Zeisel et al., 2015; Tasic et al., 2016) and have been shown to protect cortical neurons from ischemic injury (Héron-Milhavet et al., 2004; Sun et al., 2006) and to modulate their excitability (Giménez-Cassina et al., 2012) and intrinsic firing activity (Lemak et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lemak et al., 2014

claim: Neurons (n = 277) of the juvenile rat barrel cortex from layers I to IV were functionally and molecularly characterized in acute slices by scRT-PCR.
source: Neurons (n = 277) of the juvenile rat barrel cortex from layers I to IV (Supplementary file 1) were functionally and molecularly characterized in acute slices by scRT-PCR (Figure 1), whose sensitivity was validated from 500 pg of total cortical RNAs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Experimental data from the study

claim: Neurons were segregated into seven different subtypes according to their overall molecular and electrophysiological similarity using unsupervised Ward's clustering.
source: Neurons were segregated into seven different subtypes according to their overall molecular and electrophysiological similarity (Figure 1A) using unsupervised Ward's clustering (Ward, 1963), an approach we previously successfully used to classify cortical neurons (Cauli et al., 2000; Gallopin et al., 2006; Karagiannis et al., 2009).
evidence: Experimental data from the study shown in Figure 1A

claim: Regular spiking (RS, n = 63) and intrinsically bursting (IB, n = 10) cells exhibited the molecular characteristics of glutamatergic neurons, with very high single-cell detection rate (n = 69 of 73, 95%) of vesicular glutamate transporter 1 (Slc17a7).
source: Regular spiking (RS, n = 63) and intrinsically bursting (IB, n = 10) cells exhibited the molecular characteristics of glutamatergic neurons, with very high single-cell detection rate (n = 69 of 73, 95%) of vesicular glutamate transporter 1 (Slc17a7) and low detection rate (n = 7 of 73, 10%) of glutamic acid decarboxylases (Gads, Figure 1B–E and Supplementary file 2), the GABA synthesizing enzymes.
evidence: Experimental data from the study shown in Figure 1B-E

claim: RS and IB neurons showed low detection rate (n = 7 of 73, 10%) of glutamic acid decarboxylases (Gads).
source: Regular spiking (RS, n = 63) and intrinsically bursting (IB, n = 10) cells exhibited the molecular characteristics of glutamatergic neurons, with very high single-cell detection rate (n = 69 of 73, 95%) of vesicular glutamate transporter 1 (Slc17a7) and low detection rate (n = 7 of 73, 10%) of glutamic acid decarboxylases (Gads, Figure 1B–E and Supplementary file 2), the GABA synthesizing enzymes.
evidence: Experimental data from the study shown in Figure 1B-E

claim: Glutamatergic neurons displayed hyperpolarized resting membrane potential (−81.2 ± 0.8 mV).
source: This group of glutamatergic neurons distinctly displayed hyperpolarized resting membrane potential (−81.2 ± 0.8 mV), possessed a large membrane capacitance (108.6 ± 3.6 pF), discharged with wide action potentials (1.4 ± 0.0 ms) followed by medium afterhyperpolarizations (mAHs).
evidence: Experimental data from the study

claim: Glutamatergic neurons possessed a large membrane capacitance (108.6 ± 3.6 pF).
source: This group of glutamatergic neurons distinctly displayed hyperpolarized resting membrane potential (−81.2 ± 0.8 mV), possessed a large membrane capacitance (108.6 ± 3.6 pF), discharged with wide action potentials (1.4 ± 0.0 ms) followed by medium afterhyperpolarizations (mAHs).
evidence: Experimental data from the study

claim: Glutamatergic neurons discharged with wide action potentials (1.4 ± 0.0 ms) followed by medium afterhyperpolarizations (mAHs).
source: This group of glutamatergic neurons distinctly displayed hyperpolarized resting membrane potential (−81.2 ± 0.8 mV), possessed a large membrane capacitance (108.6 ± 3.6 pF), discharged with wide action potentials (1.4 ± 0.0 ms) followed by medium afterhyperpolarizations (mAHs).
evidence: Experimental data from the study

claim: Glutamatergic neurons sustained only low maximal frequencies (35.4 ± 1.6 Hz).
source: These neurons did sustain only low maximal frequencies (35.4 ± 1.6 Hz) and showed complex spike amplitude accommodation (Supplementary file 5).
evidence: Experimental data from the study

claim: All other neuronal subtypes were characterized by a high single-cell detection rate of Gad2 and/or Gad1 mRNA (n = 202 of 204, 99%) and therefore likely corresponded to GABAergic interneurons.
source: All other neuronal subtypes were characterized by a high single-cell detection rate of Gad2 and/or Gad1 mRNA (n = 202 of 204, 99%, Figure 1B and Supplementary file 2) and therefore likely corresponded to GABAergic interneurons.
evidence: Experimental data from the study shown in Figure 1B

claim: Vip interneurons were segregated into bursting Vip (n = 27) and adapting Vip (n = 59) neurons.
source: Among Gad-positive population, neurons were frequently positive for vasoactive intestinal polypeptide (Vip) mRNA, and in accordance to their electrophysiological phenotypes, were segregated into bursting Vip (n = 27) and adapting Vip (n = 59) neurons.
evidence: Experimental data from the study

claim: Vip interneurons were characterized by high membrane resistance (581 ± 27 MΩ) and small membrane capacitance (52.7 ± 2.3 pF).
source: These Vip interneurons were further characterized by high membrane resistance (581 ± 27 MΩ) and small membrane capacitance (52.7 ± 2.3 pF, Figure 1B, C and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Experimental data from the study shown in Figure 1B, C

claim: Adapting Sst neurons (n = 24) displayed depolarized resting membrane potential, pronounced voltage sags, low rheobases, and pronounced afterdepolarizations (ADs).
source: In other GABAergic interneurons somatostatin (Sst) and calbindin (Calb1) as well as neuropeptide Y (Npy) to a lesser extent were frequently detected and functionally corresponded to Adapting Sst neurons (n = 24, Figure 1B and Supplementary file 2). They displayed depolarized resting membrane potential, pronounced voltage sags, low rheobases, and pronounced afterdepolarizations (ADs; Figure 1C and Supplementary files 3; 4 and 7).
evidence: Experimental data from the study shown in Figure 1C

claim: Fast Spiking-Pvalb interneurons (FS-Pvalb, n = 37 of 38, 97%) were characterized by low membrane resistance (201 ± 13 MΩ), fast time constant, high rheobase, very short spikes (0.6 ± 0.0 ms) with sharp fast afterhyperpolarizations (fAHs) and the ability to sustain high firing rates (139.9 ± 6.8 Hz) with little to no frequency adaptation.
source: Finally, parvalbumin (Pvalb) was observed in virtually all neurons of a subpopulation termed Fast Spiking-Pvalb interneurons (FS-Pvalb, n = 37 of 38, 97%, Figure 1B and Supplementary file 2). In comparison to all other cortical neurons described above, they were characterized by low membrane resistance (201 ± 13 MΩ), fast time constant, high rheobase, very short spikes (0.6 ± 0.0 ms) with sharp fast afterhyperpolarizations (fAHs) and the ability to sustain high firing rates (139.9 ± 6.8 Hz) with little to no frequency adaptation (Figure 1C and Supplementary files 3-7).
evidence: Experimental data from the study shown in Figure 1B, C

claim: Apart from a single Adapting Npy neuron where Kcnj8 mRNA was observed, only the Kcnj11 and Abcc8 subunits were detected in cortical neurons.
source: Apart from a single Adapting Npy neuron (Figure 1D), where Kcnj8 mRNA was observed, only the Kcnj11 and Abcc8 subunits were detected in cortical neurons (in 25%, n = 63 of 248 neurons; and in 10%, n = 28 of 277 of neurons; respectively).
evidence: Experimental data from the study shown in Figure 1D

claim: Kcnj11 was detected in 25% (n = 63 of 248) of cortical neurons.
source: Apart from a single Adapting Npy neuron (Figure 1D), where Kcnj8 mRNA was observed, only the Kcnj11 and Abcc8 subunits were detected in cortical neurons (in 25%, n = 63 of 248 neurons; and in 10%, n = 28 of 277 of neurons; respectively).
evidence: Experimental data from the study

claim: Abcc8 was detected in 10% (n = 28 of 277) of cortical neurons.
source: Apart from a single Adapting Npy neuron (Figure 1D), where Kcnj8 mRNA was observed, only the Kcnj11 and Abcc8 subunits were detected in cortical neurons (in 25%, n = 63 of 248 neurons; and in 10%, n = 28 of 277 of neurons; respectively).
evidence: Experimental data from the study

claim: The single-cell detection rate of KATP channel subunits was similar between the different neuronal subtypes.
source: The single-cell detection rate was similar between the different neuronal subtypes (Figure 1F).
evidence: Experimental data from the study shown in Figure 1F

claim: Kcnj11 and Abcc8 were codetected in cortical neurons (n = 14 of 248) suggesting the expression of functional KATP channels.
source: We also codetected Kcnj11 and Abcc8 in cortical neurons (n = 14 of 248, Figure 1D) suggesting the expression of functional KATP channels.

claim: Pinacidil (100 µM) had little or no effect on current (4.1 ± 3.7 pA, p = 0.478) and membrane resistance (−9.6 ± 3.7%, p = 0.121) in identified cortical neurons (n = 18).
source: Pinacidil (100 µM), an ABCC9-preferring KATP channel opener (Inagaki et al., 1996; Moreau et al., 2005), had little or no effect on current (4.1 ± 3.7 pA, p = 0.478) and membrane resistance (−9.6 ± 3.7%, p = 0.121, Figure 2B, C).
evidence: Experimental data from the study shown in Figure 2B, C

claim: Diazoxide (300 µM) consistently induced an outward current (45.0 ± 9.6 pA, p = 4.8 × 10−5) and a decrease in membrane resistance (−34.5 ± 4.3%, p = 3.6 × 10−5) indicative of the activation of a hyperpolarizing conductance.
source: By contrast, diazoxide (300 µM), an opener acting on ABCC8 and SUR2B-containing KATP channels (Inagaki et al., 1996; Moreau et al., 2005), consistently induced an outward current (45.0 ± 9.6 pA, p = 4.8 × 10−5) and a decrease in membrane resistance (−34.5 ± 4.3%, p = 3.6 × 10−5) indicative of the activation of a hyperpolarizing conductance (Figure 2B, C).
evidence: Experimental data from the study shown in Figure 2B, C

claim: Tolbutamide (500 µM) did not change whole-cell basal current (−6.6 ± 3.0 pA, p = 0.156) or membrane resistance (20.5 ± 7.5%, p = 3.89 × 10−2).
source: The sulfonylurea tolbutamide (500 µM, Figure 2B–C), a KATP channel blocker (Ammälä et al., 1996; Isomoto et al., 1996; Gribble et al., 1997; Isomoto and Kurachi, 1997), did not change whole-cell basal current (−6.6 ± 3.0 pA, p = 0.156) or membrane resistance (20.5 ± 7.5%, p = 3.89 × 10−2).
evidence: Experimental data from the study shown in Figure 2B-C

claim: Tolbutamide dramatically reversed diazoxide effects on both current (p = 4.1 × 10−8) and membrane resistance (p = 5.8 × 10−10).
source: Conversely, tolbutamide dramatically reversed diazoxide ffects on both current (p = 4.1 × 10−8) and membrane resistance (p = 5.8 × 10−10).
evidence: Experimental data from the study

claim: All pharmacologically analyzed neurons (n = 63) exhibited a more positive whole-cell current (ΔI = 53 ± 6 pA, range: 4–228 pA) and a lower membrane resistance (ΔRm = −270 ± 31 MΩ, range: −17 to −1221 MΩ) under diazoxide than under tolbutamide.
source: All pharmacologically analyzed neurons (n = 63) exhibited a more positive whole-cell current (ΔI = 53 ± 6 pA, range: 4–228 pA) and a lower membrane resistance (ΔRm = −270 ± 31 MΩ, range: −17 to −1221 MΩ) under diazoxide than under tolbutamide, indicative of their sensitivy to KATP channel manipulation.
evidence: Experimental data from the study

claim: In virtually all neuronal subtypes or groups, the diazoxide–tolbutamide current/voltage relationship reversed very close to the theoretical potassium equilibrium potential (EK = −106.0 mV).
source: In virtually all neuronal subtypes (H(6,43) = 2.274, p = 0.810, Kruskal–Wallis H test) or groups (t(42) = 0.3395, p = 0.736, Student's t-test), the diazoxide–tolbutamide current/voltage relationship reversed very close to the theoretical potassium equilibrium potential (EK = −106.0 mV, Figure 2D–F) confirming the opening of a selective potassium conductance.
evidence: Experimental data from the study shown in Figure 2D-F

claim: MnTMPyP (25 µM), a ROS scavenger, did not reduce the diazoxide–tolbutamide responses on current (t(10)=0.76559, p = 0.462) and conductance (t(10)=1.24758, p = 0.241).
source: This possibility was ruled out by the observation that Mn(III)tetrakis(1-methyl-4-pyridyl)porphyrin (MnTMPyP, 25 µM), a ROS scavenger (D'Agostino et al., 2007), did not reduce the diazoxide–tolbutamide responses on current (t(10)=0.76559, p = 0.462, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B) and conductance (t(10)=1.24758, p = 0.241, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Experimental data from the study shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: Cortical neurons exhibited KATP conductances of similar value between their subtypes (H(6,63) = 5.6141, p = 0.468) or groups (U(9,54) = 233, p = 0.855).
source: Cortical neurons exhibited KATP conductances of similar value between their subtypes (H(6,63) = 5.6141, p = 0.468) or groups (U(9,54) = 233, p = 0.855, Mann–Whitney U test, Figure 2—figure supplement 2 A,B).
evidence: Experimental data from the study shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 A,B

claim: KATP channels activated by diazoxide essentially doubled the whole-cell conductance in the subthreshold membrane potential compared to control or tolbutamide conditions, regardless of neuronal subtypes (H(6,63) = 5.4763, p = 0.484) or groups (t(61) = 1.324, p = 0.191).
source: KATP channels activated by diazoxide essentially doubled the whole-cell conductance in the subthreshold membrane potential compared to control or tolbutamide conditions, regardless of neuronal subtypes (H(6,63) = 5.4763, p = 0.484) or groups (t(61) = 1.324, p = 0.191, Figure 2G, H).
evidence: Experimental data from the study shown in Figure 2G, H

claim: KATP current density was similar between neuronal subtypes (H(6,63) = 4.4769, p = 0.612) or groups (U(9,54) = 240.5, p = 0.965).

claim: Twenty-nine diazoxide/tolbutamide-responsive neurons were successfully characterized by scRT-PCR, with Kcnj11 and Abcc8 mRNAs detected in 35% (n = 10 of 29) and 7% (n = 2 of 29) of these neurons, respectively.
source: Twenty-nine diazoxide/tolbutamide-responsive neurons were successfully characterized by scRT-PCR. Kcnj11 and Abcc8 mRNAs were detected in 35 % (n = 10 of 29) and 7 % (n = 2 of 29) of these neurons, respectively.
evidence: Experimental data from the study

claim: The detection proportions of Kcnj11 and Abcc8 in diazoxide/tolbutamide-responsive neurons are similar to the whole sample of profiled cortical neurons (p = 0.3721 and p = 1.0000, Fisher's exact test).
source: These proportions are low compared to the pharmacological responsiveness but similar to the whole sample of profiled cortical neurons (p = 0.3721 and p = 1.0000, Fisher's exact test).
evidence: Statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: Kcnj11 and Abcc8 subunits were underdetected by scRT-PCR mRNA profiling.
source: These observations suggest that Kcnj11 and Abcc8 subunits were underdetected by scRT-PCR mRNA profiling.
evidence: Inference from the discrepancy between pharmacological responsiveness and mRNA detection

claim: The large majority of cortical neurons express functional ABCC8-mediated KATP channels across different subpopulations.
source: Together with the pinacidil unresponsiveness and the lack of Abcc9 detection, these data indicate that the large majority of cortical neurons express functional ABCC8-mediated KATP channels across different subpopulations.
evidence: Inference from pharmacological and molecular data

claim: Kcnj11 and Abcc8 subunits can be detected in pyramidal cells from wild-type mice by scRT-PCR.
source: We first verified that Kcnj11 and Abcc8 subunits can be detected in pyramidal cells from wild-type mice by scRT-PCR (Figure 3A, B).
evidence: Experimental data from the study shown in Figure 3A, B

claim: Atp1a1 and Atp1a3 were the main α-subunits of the Na+/K+ ATPase pump detected in pyramidal neurons.
source: We confirmed that Atp1a1 and Atp1a3 were the main α-subunits of the Na+/K+ ATPase pump detected in pyramidal neurons (Zeisel et al., 2015; Tasic et al., 2016).
evidence: Experimental data from the study confirmed by citations to Zeisel et al., 2015 and Tasic et al., 2016

claim: Dialysis of ATP-free/20 mM Na+-pipette solution induced an outward current in most Kcnj11+/+ neurons recorded (n = 19 out of 26; mean for n = 26: 46.7 ± 19.0 pA at −50 mV, median value = 16.2 pA, Chi2 = 5.538, p = 0.01860).
source: Dialysis of ATP-free/20 mM Na+-pipette solution induced an outward current in most Kcnj11+/+ neurons recorded (n = 19 out of 26; mean for n = 26: 46.7 ± 19.0 pA at −50 mV, median value = 16.2 pA, Chi2 = 5.538, p = 0.01860, one sample median test).

claim: In some Kcnj11+/+ neurons (n = 6 of 26), ATP-free dialysis resulted in an outward current of more than 100 pA that reversed close to EK.
source: In some neurons (n = 6 of 26), this procedure resulted in an outward current of more than 100 pA that reversed close to EK (see example in Figure 3C, F).

claim: The outward current induced by ATP-free dialysis was not observed in Kcnj11−/− neurons (U(26,22) = 78, p = 2.4221 × 10−6, one-tailed).

claim: Dialysis induced an inward current in most Kcnj11−/− neurons (n = 20 of 22; mean for n = 22: −59.9 ± 11.9 pA, median value = −61.9 pA, Chi2 = 14.727, p = 0.000124).
source: Instead, dialysis induced an inward current in most Kcnj11−/− neurons (n = 20 of 22; mean for n = 22: −59.9 ± 11.9 pA, n = 22, median value = −61.9 pA, Chi2 = 14.727, p = 0.000124, one sample median test), suggesting that other conductances than the KATP channels were also altered.
evidence: Experimental data from the study

claim: Cortical neurons predominantly express functional KATP channels composed of KCNJ11 and ABCC8 subunits.
source: Collectively, these data indicate that cortical neurons predominantly express functional KATP channels composed of KCNJ11 and ABCC8 subunits.
evidence: Inference from genetic and pharmacological data

claim: Tolbutamide resulted in a slight depolarization (ΔVm = 2.6 ± 0.8 mV, p = 1.74 × 10−2) and increase in membrane resistance (ΔRm = 78 ± 32 MΩ, p = 1.52 × 10−3) in identified cortical neurons (n = 39).
source: Following electrophysiological identification, the KATP channel blocker tolbutamide was applied, which resulted in a slight depolarization (ΔVm = 2.6 ± 0.8 mV, p = 1.74 × 10−2, Figure 4A, B) and increase in membrane resistance (ΔRm = 78 ± 32 MΩ, p = 1.52 × 10−3, Figure 4B, E).
evidence: Experimental data from the study shown in Figure 4A, B, E

claim: Tolbutamide effects were strong enough to trigger and stimulate the firing of action potentials (ΔF = 0.3 ± 0.2 Hz, p = 9.21 × 10−3).
source: These effects were strong enough to trigger and stimulate the firing of action potentials (ΔF = 0.3 ± 0.2 Hz, p = 9.21 × 10−3, Figure 4A, C, F).
evidence: Experimental data from the study shown in Figure 4A, C, F

claim: Diazoxide hyperpolarized cortical neurons (−4.0 ± 0.6 mV, p = 1.87 × 10−4) and decreased their membrane resistance (−39 ± 23 MΩ, p = 1.52 × 10−3).
source: By contrast, diazoxide hyperpolarized cortical neurons (−4.0 ± 0.6 mV, p = 1.87 × 10−4, Figure 4A, D), decreased their membrane resistance (−39 ± 23 MΩ, p = 1.52 × 10−3, Figure 4B, E) but did alter their rather silent basal spiking activity (−0.1 ± 0.1 Hz, p = 0.821, Figure 4A, C, F).

evidence: Speculation based on experimental findings and supported by citations

claim: Glutamatergic synaptic transmission stimulates blood glucose uptake, astrocyte glycolysis, as well as lactate release.

evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies
